All v2 configuration is passed to `fit()`, so separate model fits do not share
mutable global state.

## ARIMA/GARCH order

`order=(p, q, d)` controls the ARIMA mean process (AR, MA, integer differencing).
`garch_order=(k, m)`
controls the GARCH variance process. Set `vol="GARCH"` or `vol="EGARCH"`.

```{python}
#| eval: false
results = model.fit(order=(1, 0, 1), garch_order=(1, 1), vol="GARCH")
```

## ARMA exact log likelihood and RE/FE correction {#arima-likelihood-initialization}

`exact_ll` defaults to `None` (automatic):

| Value | Likelihood selection |
|---|---|
| `None` | Enable the Gaussian covariance correction for supported ARIMA models with `garch_order=(0, 0)`, including time series and panels with FE/RE. Otherwise use conditional likelihood. |
| `True` | Force the correction on, including with GARCH; unsupported specifications still raise an error. |
| `False` | Force conditional likelihood with zero presample innovations. |

`results.exact_ll` records the resolved boolean, not `None`. Automatic selection
leaves fractional, EGARCH, custom/non-Gaussian and censored models conditional.
Static models (`order=(0, 0, 0)`) also remain conditional in automatic mode.

For constant-variance ARMA without effects, this gives exact stationary Gaussian
likelihood, including the infinite AR history and all supplied regressors.
It reuses the native inverse-MA column and a stationary Lyapunov prior.
Factorizations are only `r`-by-`r`, where `r = max(p, q)`; no time-by-time
covariance is built. Work and storage grow linearly with history length for
fixed orders and parameter count. The Hessian batches its derivative solves.

The corrected density replaces the conditional density once per entity.
Analytic scores/Hessians, robust scores, whitening and forecasts use the same
covariance. Ragged groups exclude padding and integer-differencing boundaries.
After differencing this is not a diffuse likelihood for the original levels.

GARCH/effects/variance-regressor models retain the dense finite-history
approximation `C = diag(v) + v[0] * H @ H.T`. Their variance paths and effects
transforms are unchanged; this is not exact joint GARCH or marginal-effects
likelihood, and long histories can be expensive.

Fixed or random effects do not remove the need to account for each series'
unobserved history. The correction remains applicable and is enabled
automatically without GARCH. A small RE-only pilot suggested improved ARMA
parameter RMSE, although this is preliminary evidence; the retained effects
transformation does not provide exact joint integration over random effects.

Exact stationary GARCH likelihood would require integrating over unobserved
past shocks and initial volatility, whose stationary distribution generally
has no closed form. This requires specialized numerical methods and is not
implemented here. The ARMA correction alone does not provide that integration
or a reliable improvement in estimates: a small paired pilot found no
consistent RMSE gain with GARCH, with or without random effects. This is
preliminary evidence, not a general result; automatic mode keeps GARCH
models conditional.

When enabled, the option requires regular observations and the built-in Gaussian model.
Non-Gaussian/custom likelihoods, EGARCH, fractional differencing, censoring and
IV are rejected. Invalid AR roots or nonpositive/clipped variances invalidate
a trial. See the ARMA exact log likelihood and RE/FE correction section in
`paneltime_doc/main.tex` for the implemented equations.

## Evaluate without fitting

`model.prepare_likelihood(FitOptions(...))` prepares the data once and returns a
reusable evaluator. It does not optimize, build result tables, or impose a
seasonal model. All regressors in the model formula remain in the coefficient
vector, with the same analytic regression/ARMA/variance cross derivatives.

```{python}
#| eval: false
evaluator = model.prepare_likelihood(
    pt.FitOptions(order=(2, 1, 0), garch_order=(0, 0), exact_ll=True))
parameters = evaluator.initial_parameters.copy()
evaluation = evaluator.evaluate(parameters)
evaluation.loglike, evaluation.score, evaluation.hessian
```

`parameter_names` and `parameter_groups` describe the full vector, in engine
coefficient coordinates. Supply all coefficients, including fixed ones:
`evaluate` does not apply fit constraints. `derivative_order=0`, `1`, or `2`
requests density only, density and score, or all three. Invalid parameter trials
raise `ValueError`. Only the last parameter vector and its computed derivatives
are reused; returned derivative arrays are copies. Preparation uses the existing
initializer, so its warnings can still appear.

For nonlinear coefficient relationships, an external optimizer can use this
evaluator directly, without invoking `fit` at each trial. If `a = f(b)` maps
optimizer coordinates to the full vector, transform derivatives as
`g_b = J.T @ g_a` and
`H_b = J.T @ H_a @ J + sum(g_a[k] * Hessian(f[k]))`.
The second term is required for products, log variances and other nonlinear maps.
Explicitly fixing every coefficient in a final `fit` is supported: the full
vector is retained and results are constructed with zero optimization iterations.
Standard errors conditional on all coefficients being fixed are unavailable;
inference for the external coordinates must use their transformed curvature.

## Fractional differencing (ARFIMA)

Use `fractional_d="estimate"` to estimate one common fractional parameter across
entities, or pass a number strictly between `-0.5` and `0.5` to fix it.
The default `None` leaves existing behavior unchanged; fixed `0.0` is equivalent
to no fractional filtering.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# ARFIMA(1, d, 1)-GARCH(1, 1): the integer-difference entry stays zero.
results = model.fit(order=(1, 1, 0), garch_order=(1, 1),
                    fractional_d="estimate")
print(results.fractional_d)
# A fixed fractional parameter is not counted as an estimated coefficient.
fixed = model.fit(order=(1, 1, 0), fractional_d=0.25)
```

Estimated `d` appears in the parameter and standard-error tables. Its numerical
bounds are `-0.5 + 1e-8` and `0.5 - 1e-8`; constraints such as
`constraints={"d": (-0.3, 0.4)}` can narrow these bounds or fix the parameter.
`results.fractional_d` gives either the estimated or fixed value.

The conditional model filters regression residuals, including the intercept:
`(1-L)^d (Y-X beta)` is passed through the existing ARMA filter, effects
adjustment, and GARCH recursion. Fractional filtering is independent of the
innovation distribution, variance link, and custom h-function. Effects retain
their existing innovation-scale interpretation.

All available within-entity history is used, with residuals before each entity's
first observation set to zero. This is a conditional, finite-history likelihood,
not the exact stationary ARFIMA likelihood. Histories never cross entity
boundaries; unbalanced panels may have different history lengths. Each retained
entity needs at least three regularly spaced numeric or datetime observations.
Irregular observations/internal gaps and simultaneous integer differencing are
rejected explicitly. The declared sampling frequency cannot be inferred when an
entire regularly spaced series is subsampled.

One-step forecasts invert fractional differencing using the entity's full
observed residual history; the existing forecast-horizon limits still apply.
The fractional filter and its analytic derivatives currently cost quadratic time
in the longest history length, so benchmark long series before large simulations.
Standard errors at active bounds require the usual boundary-inference caution.

## Effects

Create `pt.Effects(...)` and pass it as the `effects` argument to
`Model.fit()`, not to the `Model` constructor. `group` controls entity effects,
`time` controls calendar-date effects, and `variance` controls effects in the
variance transformation. Omitted fields keep their defaults.

The complete option table below is generated by `setup_script.py` from the
same definitions used to validate fits.

{{< include ../_includes/effects-options.qmd >}}

```{python}
#| eval: false
effects = pt.Effects(group="random", time="fixed", variance="none")
model = pt.Model("Y ~ X0 + X1", data, entity="IDs", time="dates")
results = model.fit(order=(2, 2, 0), garch_order=(2, 2), effects=effects)

# Inline configuration: entity fixed effects, no time or variance effects.
fixed = model.fit(effects=pt.Effects(group="fixed"))

# Disable all effects (also the default).
pooled = model.fit(effects=pt.Effects())
```

Group and time effects are removed from the ARMA innovations, after the ARMA
filter. This is exact when the effects enter the innovations of the ARMA
process. When they are added directly to the serially correlated residuals, it
is an approximation. In simulations the resulting error was small compared with
ordinary finite-sample error.

## Optimizer and covariance

Create `pt.OptimizerOptions(...)` and pass it as the `optimizer` argument to
`Model.fit()`. These are configuration fields, not separate arguments to the
`Model` constructor or `fit()`: for example, use
`model.fit(optimizer=pt.OptimizerOptions(max_iterations=300))`, not
`model.fit(max_iterations=300)`. Omitted fields retain their defaults;
`pt.OptimizerOptions()` supplies all defaults. Settings are per fit, not global.

All available controls, including constraints, initialization, numerical
precision, reduction thresholds and covariance settings, are listed below.
Defaults, permitted values and descriptions are generated from the central
option schema whenever `setup_script.py` runs its normal build workflow.

{{< include ../_includes/optimizer-options.qmd >}}

Both conventional and robust standard
errors are available on the returned results object as `bse` and
`robust_bse`; `bse_at(params)` evaluates robust standard errors at supplied
parameter values. The `cov_type` keyword is accepted by `Model.fit()` but does
not currently select between these covariance results.

```{python}
#| eval: false
optimizer = pt.OptimizerOptions(
    tolerance=1e-5,
    max_iterations=300,
    robust_cov_lags=(100, 30),
    garch_ridge_wald=0,  # Disable automatic GARCH ridge reduction.
)
results = model.fit(
    order=(2, 2, 0),
    garch_order=(2, 2),
    effects=pt.Effects(group="random", time="random"),
    optimizer=optimizer,
)

# You can also update a configuration object before passing it to fit().
optimizer.max_iterations = 500
refit = model.fit(optimizer=optimizer)
```

For most fits, start with the defaults and adjust `max_iterations` or
`tolerance` if needed. Other fields are advanced controls; changing
`garch_assist` or `kurtosis_adj` also changes the likelihood, not merely the
optimization algorithm. Invalid settings raise an error when the fit is
prepared. See the sections below for reduction and initialization details.

### GARCH ridge reduction

Automatic ARMA common-factor and GARCH ridge reductions require **both**
their Wald criterion and matching condition-index evidence from the current
Hessian on free parameters. A dimension must have CI >=
`OptimizerOptions.multicoll_threshold_report` (default 30), with
variance-decomposition proportions > 0.5 for at least one free AR and one
free MA coefficient (ARMA), or at least two free gamma lags (GARCH), in that
same dimension. CI from unrelated parameters is insufficient. Raising this
option therefore affects reduction eligibility as well as reporting.
CI uses absolute eigenvalues and does not by itself establish concavity.

`OptimizerOptions.garch_ridge_wald` defaults to `0.2` and accepts finite
non-negative real numbers (not booleans). Set it to `0` to disable automatic
GARCH ridge reduction:

```{python}
#| eval: false
optimizer = pt.OptimizerOptions(garch_ridge_wald=0)
results = model.fit(optimizer=optimizer)
```

For converged or stalled fits with at least two free gamma lags, the detector
uses the squared Wald statistic `W = far**2 / variance`. Here `far` is the
distance from the highest free gamma coefficient to the farther endpoint
(zero or total free gamma persistence), and `variance` is that coefficient's
diagonal entry in the pseudoinverse of the negative Hessian.
If the variance is nonzero and `abs(W) < garch_ridge_wald`, the highest free
gamma lag is fixed at zero and the model is
refitted. The reduction is retained only if the refit converges and
`2 * (original_loglik - reduced_loglik) <= 3.841`, the 5% chi-square(1)
critical value. Otherwise the previous fit and constraints are restored.
Accepted reductions are listed in the optimizer message.
With negative variance, the absolute ratio is used only as a ridge heuristic,
not a valid Wald test or proof of a flat ridge. Zero variance is skipped.

After accepting a reduction, the optimizer releases the newly fixed gamma
lag and retries from the reduced solution once. This uses the remaining
`max_iterations` budget; earlier automatic reductions and user constraints
remain in force. The released fit is retained only if it converges, has a
negative-definite Hessian on free parameters, has no detected gamma ridge,
and has likelihood no lower than either the original or reduced fit.
Otherwise the reduced fit and constraints are restored. An accepted release
ends the reduction loop, and the optimizer message records the release.
No restrictions are toggled during individual optimizer iterations.

The threshold is not a number of standard errors or a continuous ridge
penalty. Larger values make reduction attempts more likely, subject to the
same likelihood-ratio check. Fixed coefficients change the fitted model;
their standard errors should not be compared as if all requested lags were
still freely estimated.

### Automatic starting values

When AR or MA terms are requested, the default single start uses the full
requested order. An OLS regression is followed by Hannan--Rissanen-style
auxiliary regressions and a short conditional-sum-of-squares (CSS) refinement
of the regression and ARMA coefficients. The preliminary fit ignores GARCH;
its innovations supply the initial innovation variance and the existing
GARCH moment starts. No additional dependency is required.
CSS refinement is limited to 10 iterations and stops early at a scaled
gradient of `1e-4` or a relative objective improvement of `1e-4`; it supplies
a useful neighborhood, not a precise standalone ARMA estimate.

Internally, `arma_start.fit_arma(panel)` coordinates the working regression,
scaling, auxiliary-regression seed, CSS refinement, and conversion back to
original units. Orders, observation masks, differencing boundaries, and
preliminary effects settings come from the panel object. The numerical
filtering and optimization steps are separate helpers; initialization does
not modify the panel's data or masks.
Innovations and their derivative channels are filtered using the existing C
ARMA recursion. Each contiguous observation run is packed as an independent
series, preserving zero-presample resets at gaps and differencing boundaries.
This reuses the shipped native library without a new compiled entry point.

The CSS fit uses analytic first derivatives and reflection coordinates to
keep its preliminary ARMA coefficients stationary and invertible. These
safeguards do not change the final likelihood's constraints or Hessian.
Panel runs are filtered separately, with no lags crossing group boundaries.
For effects models, this preliminary fit uses fixed, pre-transformed working
data; the final likelihood still removes effects after ARMA filtering.
An underidentified auxiliary regression, CSS iteration limit, or numerical
stall produces an `ARMAInitializationWarning` rather than being presented as
successful preliminary convergence. It does not abort the final likelihood
fit: the best accepted preliminary coefficients remain usable. Other numerical
warnings are still treated as errors. CSS damping adapts to the actual versus
predicted objective reduction, not merely whether a step decreases the objective.

Models without ARMA terms retain their existing OLS initialization. Explicit
starting arguments supplied through the engine bypass the automatic CSS fit.
Like any single-start initialization, this does not guarantee a global
likelihood maximum.

### Local single-start execution

Fitting runs locally. Legacy node dispatch and GUI/browser progress channels
have been removed, as has the `Model(..., multiprocess=...)` argument. Final
summaries, inference, diagnostics and predictions remain available.

`execute` prepares the panel once and passes its initial parameters directly
to the shared likelihood optimizer. `processing/initreg.py` selects ordinary
static FE/RE starts during panel initialization, in the same place as the
ARMA/GARCH starts. Mixed fixed/random effects,
explicit constraints (including `{}`), censoring, variance regressors/effects,
instruments and custom likelihoods/functions retain their existing starts.
Explicit engine starts are not replaced. Every fit uses `dfpmax` and the
same inference, diagnostics and forecasts. A converged initial point returns
without a line search (`optim_result.its == 0`); otherwise the optimizer
refines the starting estimates. Iterations count completed optimizer steps.
Automatic starting values, explicit engine starting arguments,
and coefficient constraints are retained. The `multistart` optimizer option
and `optim_result.multistart_results` have been removed. The fit reports its
own convergence status; it does not search or select among alternative starts.

### Gaussian RE likelihood audit

An analytical Hessian differentiates the implemented criterion; it does not
establish that the criterion is the marginal likelihood of the stated model.
The reproducible audit reference in
[`tests/re_likelihood_reference.py`](../../tests/re_likelihood_reference.py)
examines the simpler stationary Gaussian model

$$
y_{it}-x_{it}'\beta=a_i+c_t+u_{it},\qquad
u_{it}=\rho u_{i,t-1}+\epsilon_{it},
$$

where the three innovation/effect families are independent, with variances
$\sigma^2,\tau_a^2,\tau_c^2$. For entity-major stacking,

$$
\Sigma =
 I_N\otimes\left\{\frac{\sigma^2}{1-\rho^2}
    [\rho^{|s-t|}]_{s,t=1}^T\right\}
 +\tau_a^2 I_N\otimes J_T+\tau_c^2 J_N\otimes I_T,
$$

where $J_k$ is the $k$-by-$k$ all-ones matrix. Its exact marginal log-likelihood is

$$
\ell_{\rm exact}
=-\tfrac12\{NT\log(2\pi)+\log|\Sigma|+r'\Sigma^{-1}r\}.
$$

The reference checks dense Cholesky evaluation against an independent
AR-innovations/Woodbury evaluation integrating out both effects.
For a true covariance $\Sigma_0$, expectations require no simulated data:

$$
E_0[\ell_{\rm exact}(\Sigma)]
=-\tfrac12\{NT\log(2\pi)+\log|\Sigma|
                  +\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_0)\}.
$$

The package instead applies the AR filter, quasi-demeans the filtered
innovations, and sums univariate normal contributions. In this special case,
with weights frozen, write $A=I-\theta_a P_a-\theta_c P_c$, where $P_a,P_c$
project onto centered group and time means, $B=I_N\otimes(I_T-\rho L_T)$, and
let $D$ contain the variances used in those contributions. Then

$$
\ell_Q=-\tfrac12\{NT\log(2\pi)+\log|D|
                         +r'B'A'D^{-1}AB r\},
$$

and its expectation replaces the last quadratic form by
$\operatorname{tr}(D^{-1}AB\Sigma_0B'A')$. The frozen weights use the moments
of the filtered components: innovation variance $\sigma^2$, filtered group
effect $a_i(1-\rho)$ and filtered time effect $c_t-\rho c_{t-1}$.
The tests reproduce the package transformation, likelihood, and AR score on a
deterministic panel, accounting for its $10^{-8}$ squared-residual stabilizer.

Two separate qualifications matter:

- Even for a fixed invertible transformation, a density for the original
  residuals requires the transformation's log determinant. With frozen
  weights that determinant is constant with respect to $\rho$, so adding it
  alone cannot correct a nonzero expected AR score. With residual-adaptive
  weights, the transformation's Jacobian also includes derivatives of those
  weights; it is not simply $|A|$.
- Scalar quasi-demeaning generally does not give
  $AB\Sigma_0B'A'=D$ for serially correlated disturbances: the first period is
  not filtered, and the filtered time effect is serially correlated. The
  package preserves the grand mean; correcting that direction is sufficient for
  the iid benchmark with known variances, but still does not whiten the AR(1)
  cases.

For $N=4,T=8,\rho=0.5,\sigma^2=2,\tau_a^2=\tau_c^2=1$, with theoretical
moment-based weights fixed and the first variance fixed at
$\sigma^2/(1-\rho^2)$, the expected scores in the coordinates
$(\rho,\log\sigma^2)$ are approximately $(1.6299,0.9500)$ for $\ell_Q$ and
$(0,0)$ for the exact marginal likelihood. Without effects, the whitening and
zero-score checks pass.

**Scope:** the package recomputes its weights from residuals, whereas this
expectation calculation freezes theoretical weights. It is not the expected
score of the complete residual-adaptive estimator, a proof of its asymptotic
bias, or a GARCH likelihood replacement. It establishes a concrete mismatch
with the exact Gaussian marginal benchmark and explains why a determinant-only
patch is insufficient. The production RE likelihood is unchanged pending a
validated treatment of the full dynamic/heteroskedastic model.

From the package root, run `python tests\re_likelihood_reference.py` for the
JSON audit report, or `python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test*py" -v`
for its regression checks and the package tests.

## Constraints

Use `constraints=` for coefficient restrictions and `add_intercept`,
`subtract_means`, `tobit_limits`, and `suppress_output` for
fit behavior.

## Custom model and h-function

Pass a likelihood instance with `likelihood=` or a SymPy expression with
`h_function=`. See the [custom likelihood guide](../guide/custom-likelihood-models.qmd)
and [heteroskedasticity guide](../guide/heteroskedasticity-functions.qmd).

## Migrating from `pt.options`

| v1 | v2 |
|---|---|
| `pqdkm` | `order=` and `garch_order=` |
| `EGARCH` | `vol="EGARCH"` |
| `fixed_random_group_eff`, `fixed_random_time_eff`, `fixed_random_variance_eff` | `effects=pt.Effects(...)` |
| `custom_model` | `likelihood=` (an instance) |
| `user_constraints` | `constraints=` |
| `use_analytical` | No corresponding v2 option; the current implementation uses analytical derivatives. |
| `supress_output` | `suppress_output=` |
